passage: Gopika, since you keep telling me you don't want to be pushy, let old Ujjwal tell you about my rule. When I was twenty-one I wrote to an engineer and heard nothing. I did not know whether to write again or drop it. I stayed awake over it. Then a senior said, "Make a rule beforehand, so your head doesn't argue." Mine was: if there is no answer in a week, I send one short, polite follow-up. After that, I let it go and think no worse of anyone. A week passed. I sent two lines: "Just checking that my message did not get buried. No worries if the timing is bad." No reply. I closed the tab and felt calm. Three months later that same engineer nodded to me at a conference and said, "Sorry, I missed it. Ask me now."

qa.q: How long did Ujjwal's rule say to wait before following up?
qa.a: Ujjwal's rule said to wait a week.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling before the rule was made?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt unsettled and stuck, unsure whether to write again and lying awake over it.

qa.q: What choice inside the story kept Ujjwal calm after no reply, and why?
qa.a: Ujjwal made the rule beforehand and closed the tab once it was used, because the decision was already made and there was nothing left to argue with oneself about.

qa.q: How might the engineer have seen the follow-up?
qa.a: The engineer received a short, polite note with no pressure, which may explain the friendly remark at the conference months later.

grounding: Shows an if-then plan for following up once after a week and then moving on without resentment.

passage:
Ritu wrote to Sahil, an urban planner whose article on bus lanes she had quoted in her project, on the first Monday of exam season. Before sending, she wrote a line in her planner: 'No reply by next Monday? Send one polite follow-up. Still nothing? Move on, no hard feelings.'
Exams swallowed the week. Twice she caught herself checking her inbox between papers and made herself put the phone away. The plan was already made.
Next Monday: nothing. At 9 a.m., as written, she sent two lines: 'Just bringing this to the top of your inbox in case it got buried. Completely understand if you're busy.'
Another week passed. Silence. Ritu crossed out Sahil's name, put a small tick beside it, and felt surprisingly light. She added the next name to the list, a transport researcher in Kolkata, and turned back to her revision.

qa.q: What did Ritu write in her planner before sending?
qa.a: No reply by next Monday? Send one polite follow-up. Still nothing? Move on, no hard feelings.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel after crossing out Sahil's name, and why?
qa.a: She felt surprisingly light, because the plan had already decided the next step, so the silence did not turn into resentment.

qa.q: What else could Ritu do with the next contact?
qa.a: Use the same if-then plan and keep the first message short with one clear question, so each attempt costs little.

qa.q: How might Sahil see the follow-up if the first message was buried?
qa.a: Sahil would likely find it polite and easy to handle, since it offers an easy way to say no and adds no pressure.

grounding: Shows a student setting an if-then rule, one follow-up after a week of silence and then moving on, which keeps silence from turning into resentment.

passage:
On a Sunday night in his Kolkata flat, Samir finally messaged Raghav Sen, a game designer whose talk he had watched three times. Then he opened his phone's reminders and set one for the following Sunday: 'If no reply, send one follow-up. After that, let it go.'
All week, between classes and his shift at the print shop, he felt the urge to check. The reminder helped; there was nothing to decide until Sunday.
Sunday came with no reply. Samir sent a short follow-up: 'Hi again, sharing this once more in case it slipped past. No worries at all if you're busy.' He noticed a small sour thought, he could at least say no, and let it pass. The plan said move on.
Three days later, Raghav replied: 'Sorry, I was away at a festival. Your question is a good one. Call on Friday?' Samir laughed out loud in the metro.

qa.a: If no reply, send one follow-up. After that, let it go.

qa.q: What was the small sour thought Samir noticed, and what does it show?
qa.a: The thought that Raghav could at least say no shows a flash of resentment, which Samir noticed and let pass instead of acting on.

qa.q: What would you advise Samir if the follow-up had also gone unanswered?
qa.a: Move on as planned, without bitterness, and choose another designer to contact, keeping the same one-week rule.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel on seeing the follow-up after the festival?
qa.a: Raghav might feel grateful for the reminder and relieved that it was polite, which makes it easy to reply and suggest a call.

grounding: Shows a student deciding in advance on one follow-up after a week of silence, which keeps checking and resentment in check until a reply comes.
